title: Stroke Is Striking Younger Adults, and Every Minute of Delay Costs Brain
excerpt: On World Stroke Day, doctors in Hyderabad and Delhi warn cases in under-45s have risen 40-50%, younger patients are now 20-30% of all strokes, and 1.9 million brain cells die per minute untreated.
body:
• Doctors marking World Stroke Day on October 29 warn stroke is rising fastest in adults under 45 — up 40-50% in younger people over two to three decades — and people under 45 now account for 20-30% of all stroke cases in India.
  • About 1.9 million brain cells die for every minute a stroke goes untreated; clot-busting treatment works best within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, so the practical target is a stroke-ready hospital within the first 'golden hour'.
  • Know BE FAST — Balance loss, Eye changes, Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services (911 in the US, 108 in India) — and note the exact time symptoms started; do not give food, drink or aspirin before doctors identify the stroke type.
  • Absolute risk in plain terms: roughly 1 in 4 people aged 25 and over — about 25% — will have a stroke in their lifetime, and stroke is India's fourth-leading cause of death.

Stroke is no longer mainly a disease of old age. Doctors in Hyderabad, Delhi and Bengaluru used World Stroke Day, observed on October 29, to warn that cases are climbing in younger and middle-aged adults, and that the outcome of a stroke is now decided less by the treatment available than by how quickly the patient reaches it.

The scale is large. More than 12.2 million new strokes occur worldwide each year — one every 40 seconds, with one stroke death every four minutes — according to Dr Anup Kumar Thacker, director of neurology at Medanta Hospital, speaking to ANI. Stroke is the fourth-leading cause of death and fifth-leading cause of disability in India. The shift in age is the sharper trend: incidence in people under 45 has risen 40-50% over the last two to three decades, and younger patients now make up 20-30% of all cases, Dr Thacker said. In Hyderabad, Dr K. S. V. Surya Teja Reddy, chief consultant interventional neuroradiologist at KIMS Hospitals, Kondapur, said his outpatient practice sees around 15 stroke patients a month, including a considerable number of middle-aged people.

Why younger brains are at risk

The drivers doctors named are familiar conditions arriving earlier in life: uncontrolled high blood pressure — the single most important modifiable risk factor — diabetes, high cholesterol, obesity, smoking, physical inactivity, irregular working hours, prolonged sitting and poor sleep. Heart conditions, particularly atrial fibrillation, add risk because clots formed in the heart can travel to the brain. Environmental exposure matters too: Padma Shri Dr MV Padma Srivastava of Paras Health, Gurugram, said chronic PM2.5 exposure triggers inflammation and vascular damage that raises ischemic stroke risk, and noted Delhi's PM2.5 levels run 10-15 times WHO-recommended limits. Globally, about one in four people aged 25 and above will experience a stroke in their lifetime — an absolute lifetime risk of roughly 25%, not a marginal one.

"Millions — approximately 1.9 million — of neurons or brain cells die every minute after the onset of stroke symptoms. Therefore, every minute counts."

— Dr Anup Kumar Thacker, Director of Neurology, Medanta Hospital

Every minute matters — literally

A stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked by a clot (ischemic stroke) or a vessel ruptures (haemorrhagic stroke). Deprived of oxygen, brain cells die rapidly, and the damage — paralysis, speech loss, death — grows with every minute of delay, Express Healthcare reported in its World Stroke Day briefing. Yet many patients still arrive late because early signs are mistaken for fatigue or dizziness, families wait to see if symptoms pass, or home remedies come first.

Treatment is a race against fixed windows. Intravenous thrombolysis — clot-busting drugs such as alteplase or tenecteplase — is generally given within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, and works best the earlier it starts. Mechanical thrombectomy, in which a catheter removes a large clot from a major brain artery, can help carefully selected patients up to 24 hours after they were last known well, guided by advanced CT and MRI imaging. Neither window is a reason to wait: both sources stress that earlier intervention preserves more brain. The CDC's stroke guidance makes the same point — the treatments that work best depend on recognition and diagnosis within the first hours.

What to do, and what to check this week

Use BE FAST: sudden loss of Balance, sudden Eye or vision changes, Face drooping on one side, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty — then Time: call emergency services immediately (911 in the United States, 108 in India), note when symptoms began, and go to a stroke-ready hospital. If symptoms vanish within minutes, treat it as an emergency anyway: that pattern can be a transient ischemic attack, a warning that a major stroke may follow. Do not give food, drink or aspirin — swallowing may be impaired, and if the stroke is caused by bleeding, aspirin can make it worse.

Prevention is the other half of the message, and it is measurable. Check blood pressure regularly and keep it controlled, monitor blood sugar and cholesterol, stop tobacco, limit salt, stay physically active, and treat heart conditions as prescribed. For adults in their 30s and 40s who assume stroke is a problem for their parents' generation, the doctors' World Stroke Day advice reduces to one action: get a blood-pressure, sugar and cholesterol check now, rather than after the first symptom makes the decision for you.
